name: Warehouse and Logistics Careers
objectives: Given a list of warehouse job ads, identify the job roles, what each one does and the credentials that help you get hired, naming at least four roles and one real credential with who grants it
Given a pick list with SKUs and location codes, find each item's location and put the picks in walking order, with every location read correctly
Given a practice delivery and its packing list, check in the shipment and write up any shortage, overage or damage, with every count and note correct
Given boxes with their weights, plan a safe pallet load with heavy items low and within the weight limit, meeting every rule on the pallet checklist
Given a warehouse task or hazard, choose the safe way to lift, move or report it while keeping pace, getting at least 4 of 5 situations right

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Warehouse jobs and the credentials that help
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Identify the main warehouse jobs and one credential that can help you get hired.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of warehouse job ads, you will identify the job roles, what each one does and the credentials that help you get hired, naming at least four roles and one real credential with who grants it.
Common entry jobs: material handler or warehouse associate (moving goods), picker and packer (filling customer orders), stocker or order filler, shipping and receiving clerk (checking goods in and out), inventory clerk (counting and fixing records) and forklift operator. With experience you can become a lead, a supervisor or an inventory or logistics coordinator.
Most entry jobs need no degree. People usually learn on the job, often in a month or less, and learn safety rules based on OSHA standards. Employers look for people who show up on time, count carefully and work safely.
Credentials can help you stand out. The Manufacturing Skill Standards Council (MSSC) offers the Certified Logistics Associate (CLA) and the Certified Logistics Technician (CLT); you pass the CLA before you take the CLT. OSHA's 10-hour Outreach class gives you a completion card; it is voluntary, and OSHA says it is not a certification. Forklift operation always needs the employer's own training and evaluation.
Pay and job openings differ by place. Check the official Occupational Outlook Handbook at bls.gov for pay and outlook, and real job ads near you.
Words to know:
- Logistics: planning and moving goods from where they are made to where they are needed.
- Distribution center: a large warehouse that ships goods out to stores or customers.
- Credential: a certificate or card that shows you passed a test or finished training.
- MSSC: the Manufacturing Skill Standards Council, a national group that gives the CLA and CLT credentials.
Official sources:
- U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics: Hand laborers and material movers
- U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics: Material recording clerks
- MSSC: Certified Logistics Technician (CLT) and Certified Logistics Associate (CLA)
- OSHA Outreach Training Program (10-hour and 30-hour classes)
Try it now: Find three warehouse job ads near you. For each, write the job title, the shift, what the job does in one line, and any credential or skill it asks for. Then open the MSSC CLT page and write who grants the CLA and CLT.
You can now name the main warehouse jobs, what each does, and the credentials that can help you get hired.

check.q: Which job checks goods coming in and going out against the paperwork?
check.why: Shipping and receiving clerks track incoming and outgoing shipments and check them.

check.q: Who grants the Certified Logistics Technician (CLT) credential?
check.why: The CLT, and the CLA that comes first, are MSSC credentials.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: The flow of goods and location codes
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find an item using its SKU and location code, and put picks in walking order.
This lesson builds toward: Given a pick list with SKUs and location codes, you will find each item's location and put the picks in walking order, with every location read correctly.
Goods move through a warehouse in the same order every day. Receiving: goods arrive and are checked. Putaway: they are stored in a set place. Storage. Picking: workers pull items for an order. Packing. Shipping: orders leave on trucks.
Every product has a SKU (stock keeping unit), a code for that exact item, for example a blue shirt in size large. Every storage spot has a location code. Many warehouses use zone, aisle, rack (or bay) and level, so A-12-03-B could mean zone A, aisle 12, rack 3, level B. Your warehouse will teach you its own pattern.
Most warehouses use scanners. You scan the location and the item so the computer system (a warehouse management system) knows what moved. If the item in the spot does not match the SKU, stop and tell your lead; do not grab something that looks close.
To save steps, pick in walking order: sort your list by aisle, then by rack, so you walk each aisle once.
Step by step:
- Read the SKU and the location code for each line.
- Split the location code into its parts: zone, aisle, rack, level.
- Sort the list by zone, then aisle, then rack.
- At each spot, scan or check that the SKU matches before you pick.
- If it does not match or the spot is empty, report it.
Words to know:
- SKU: stock keeping unit: a code for one exact product.
- Location code: the address of a storage spot, such as zone, aisle, rack and level.
- Putaway: moving received goods to their storage spot.
- Picking: pulling items from storage to fill an order.
- Warehouse management system (WMS): the computer system that tracks where every item is.
Official sources:
- U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics: Material recording clerks
Try it now: Practice only. Put this pick list in walking order (zone, aisle, rack, level): B-04-02-A, A-12-03-B, A-03-01-C, B-01-05-A, A-12-01-A. Then write what each part of A-12-03-B means. Check: the order starts A-03-01-C, A-12-01-A, A-12-03-B.
You can now read a location code, find an item by its SKU and put a pick list in walking order.

options: A code for one exact product
check.why: A stock keeping unit is a code for one exact item.

check.q: You go to a location and the item does not match the SKU on your list. What do you do?
options: Skip the line and say nothing
Stop and report it to your lead
check.why: A mismatch must be reported so the order and the records stay right.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Checking in a shipment and counting stock
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Check a delivery against its packing list and write up any problem.
This lesson builds toward: Given a practice delivery and its packing list, you will check in the shipment and write up any shortage, overage or damage, with every count and note correct.
When a truck arrives, receiving checks that what came is what was ordered. You compare the goods with the packing list (and the purchase order, if you have it). The driver also hands over a bill of lading, the shipping paper you sign.
Count every line. Check the SKU, the quantity and the condition. If a box is crushed, wet or open, take a photo if your site allows and write it down. If you got fewer than listed, it is a shortage; more is an overage. Write every problem on the paperwork before you sign, as your site's process says. Signing a clean receipt can mean you accepted everything as fine.
Inventory counts work the same way. A cycle count is counting a few locations each day instead of the whole warehouse at once. If your count does not match the system, count again, then report it. Accuracy matters more than speed here.
Step by step:
- Get the packing list (and purchase order if you have it).
- Count each line: right SKU, right quantity.
- Check the condition of every box.
- Write each shortage, overage or damage on the paperwork.
- Follow your site's process before signing the bill of lading.
- Report problems to your lead.
Words to know:
- Packing list: a list of what is in a shipment.
- Purchase order (PO): the buyer's order showing what was bought and how many.
- Bill of lading (BOL): the shipping paper the carrier gives; signing it says you received the goods.
- Shortage: fewer items arrived than the paperwork says.
- Overage: more items arrived than the paperwork says.
- Cycle count: counting a few locations at a time to keep records right.
Official sources:
- U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics: Material recording clerks
Try it now: Practice only. The packing list says: SKU 1001, 12 cases; SKU 1002, 8 cases; SKU 1003, 20 cases. You count 12 of 1001, 6 of 1002, and 21 of 1003, with one 1003 case crushed. Write a receiving report: each line, what was expected, what came, and the problem. Answer: 1002 short 2; 1003 over 1 and 1 damaged.
You can now check a delivery against its packing list and write up shortages, overages and damage.

check.q: The packing list says 10 cases, but 8 arrived. What is this called?
check.why: Fewer items than the paperwork lists is a shortage.

check.q: One box in a delivery is wet and torn. What do you do?
options: Note the damage on the paperwork before signing, as your site's process says
Sign the paper and say nothing
check.why: Damage must be written up so it can be claimed and not blamed on the warehouse.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Working safely and getting hired

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Safe lifting and warehouse hazards
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose the safe way to lift, move and report hazards in a warehouse.
This lesson builds toward: Given a warehouse task or hazard, you will choose the safe way to lift, move or report it while keeping pace, getting at least 4 of 5 situations right.
OSHA names the main warehouse hazards: forklifts and other powered trucks, lifting and repetitive strain, material handling, chemicals, slips, trips and falls, and robots and conveyors. The most common injuries are strains from lifting and being struck by forklifts.
Lift smart. Plan the lift and the path. Get close to the load, bend your knees, keep your back straight and the load near your body, and do not twist: turn with your feet. Use a cart, a hand truck or a pallet jack when you can. For heavy or awkward items, ask for a team lift.
Around equipment: stay in walkways, make eye contact with forklift drivers, and never walk under raised forks. Keep hands away from moving conveyors. In heat, drink water often, take your breaks and tell someone if you feel dizzy or sick.
Pace matters, but never take a shortcut that is unsafe. Report hazards like spills, damaged racks or blocked exits to your lead right away.
Step by step:
- Plan: how heavy, where to, is the path clear?
- Get close, bend your knees, back straight.
- Lift with your legs, load close to your body.
- Turn with your feet; do not twist.
- Use a cart or pallet jack, or ask for a team lift, for heavy loads.
- Report hazards right away.
Words to know:
- Ergonomics: fitting the work to the body to prevent strain and injury.
- Pallet jack: a hand-pushed or powered tool that lifts and moves pallets a short way.
- Team lift: two or more people lifting one heavy or awkward item together.
- Heat illness: sickness from working in heat, such as heat exhaustion or heat stroke.
Official sources:
- OSHA: Warehousing
- OSHA: Warehousing hazards and solutions
- OSHA: Heat exposure
Try it now: Practice with an empty or lightly packed box at home. Lift it using every step, and say each step out loud. Then write three hazards you might see in a warehouse and what you would do about each one.
You can now lift and move items safely and report warehouse hazards the right way.

check.q: You need to turn while carrying a box. How do you do it?
options: Lift it over your head first
check.why: Turning with your feet protects your back; twisting while lifting causes injury.

check.q: You see a forklift coming down your aisle. What is safest?
options: Stay in the walkway and make eye contact with the driver
Wave and keep walking in its path
check.why: Walkways and eye contact help the driver see you and keep you out of its path.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Building a safe pallet load
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Plan a pallet load with heavy items low, even layers and a total within the weight limit.
This lesson builds toward: Given boxes with their weights, you will plan a safe pallet load with heavy items low and within the weight limit, meeting every rule on the pallet checklist.
A good pallet arrives in one piece and keeps people safe. First check the pallet itself: no broken boards or nails sticking out.
Heavy boxes go on the bottom, lighter ones on top. Make even, flat layers. Keep boxes inside the pallet's edges (no hanging over). Turn every other layer so the boxes cross over each other (this is called interlocking); it helps the stack hold together. Keep under your site's height and weight limits.
Add up the weight. Example (practice only): 20 boxes at 25 lb each is 500 lb, plus a pallet of about 40 lb is 540 lb. Check it is under the limit for the pallet, the rack and the equipment.
Wrap the load with stretch wrap, tight from bottom to top, and wrap it to the pallet. Put labels facing out where they can be scanned. Before trucks are loaded, the trailer's brakes are set and its wheels are chocked; loads are spread evenly inside the trailer.
Step by step:
- Check the pallet: no broken boards or nails.
- Heaviest boxes on the bottom layer.
- Even layers, inside the edges, interlocked.
- Add up the total weight and check the limits.
- Stretch wrap tightly, bottom to top, including the pallet.
- Labels facing out.
Words to know:
- Pallet: a flat wooden or plastic base that goods are stacked on so they can be moved together.
- Interlocking: turning each layer of boxes so they overlap the layer below.
- Overhang: boxes hanging over the edge of the pallet.
- Stretch wrap: thin plastic film wrapped around a load to hold it together.
Official sources:
- OSHA: Warehousing hazards and solutions
- OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178: Powered industrial trucks (trailer brakes and wheel chocks)
Try it now: Practice only. You have 8 boxes of 50 lb, 12 boxes of 20 lb and 6 boxes of 10 lb. Sketch the pallet from the side: which boxes go on which layer. Add up the total weight with a 40 lb pallet and check it is under a 1,000 lb limit. Answer: 400 + 240 + 60 + 40 = 740 lb.
You can now plan a safe pallet load with heavy items low, even layers and a total within the limit.

check.q: Where do the heaviest boxes go on a pallet?
check.why: Heavy items low keep the load stable and protect lighter boxes.

check.q: Practice: 30 boxes at 20 lb on a 40 lb pallet. What is the total weight?
check.why: 30 x 20 = 600 lb, plus the 40 lb pallet = 640 lb.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Getting hired and moving up
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a plan to get hired with employers, a credential goal and honest résumé lines.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of warehouse job ads, you will identify the job roles, what each one does and the credentials that help you get hired, naming at least four roles and one real credential with who grants it. Given a warehouse task or hazard, you will choose the safe way to lift, move or report it while keeping pace, getting at least 4 of 5 situations right.
Where to look: large retailers' and shippers' career sites, local job boards, staffing agencies and your local American Job Center, which can also help pay for training and credentials in some cases. Many warehouses hire people with records; ask the job center about second-chance employers.
What employers want: being on time, careful counting, safe habits and steady pace. Warehouses often measure your rate, such as picks per hour. Meet it by working smart (walking order, scanning carefully) and never by skipping safety.
Make your résumé match the job. Use action words and real examples: "Counted and checked deliveries against packing lists" or "Completed warehouse safety and logistics training (Koach Learn), 2026". Veterans: supply, motor pool and logistics duties count, so put them in everyday words.
Plan your growth. A credential like the MSSC CLA, then CLT, and employer forklift training can lead to higher-paid roles such as lead, inventory control or logistics coordinator.
Step by step:
- List three employers or programs near you, including your American Job Center.
- Pick a credential goal (for example the MSSC CLA) and a target date.
- Write two honest résumé lines from this course or past work.
- Practice a 30-second answer: "How do you keep accurate and safe at a fast pace?"
Words to know:
- Rate: how much work you do in a set time, such as picks per hour.
- American Job Center: a free public office that helps people find jobs and training.
- Second-chance employer: a business that hires people with criminal records.
Official sources:
- CareerOneStop: find an American Job Center near you
- MSSC: Certified Logistics Technician (CLT) and Certified Logistics Associate (CLA)
- U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics: Hand laborers and material movers
Try it now: Write your hiring plan: three employers or programs near you, your credential goal and date, two honest résumé lines, and your 30-second answer to "How do you stay accurate and safe at a fast pace?" Read the answer out loud.
You can now write a plan to get hired in a warehouse, with a credential goal and honest résumé lines.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Receiving report A count is wrong or a shortage, overage or damage is missing. Every line shows expected and received, and every problem is written up. Also notes what to do before signing the bill of lading and who to tell. Pick list in walking order Locations are out of order or a code is read wrong. All picks sorted by zone, aisle, rack and level, with each code read right. Explains what to do if an item does not match or a spot is empty. Pallet load plan Heavy boxes high, overhang, or the total weight is wrong or over the limit. Heavy boxes low, even interlocked layers, correct total under the limit, wrapped and labeled. Adds the pallet check and the trailer safety steps. Hiring plan No employers, no credential goal, or a résumé line that claims something untrue. Three employers or programs, a real credential with who grants it and a date, two honest résumé lines. Includes a practiced 30-second answer about accuracy and safety. Safe work The plan suggests unsafe shortcuts to meet a rate. The 30-second answer and plan put safety first, with safe lifting and hazard reporting. Names a specific hazard from OSHA's warehousing page and how to prevent it. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and check again.

check.q: You are behind your picks-per-hour rate. What is the right way to catch up?
options: Pick in walking order and scan carefully
Climb the racks instead of using a ladder
check.why: Working smart saves time; unsafe shortcuts cause injuries and errors.

check.q: Which résumé line is honest and strong?
options: "MSSC CLT certified" (before you have passed it)
"Counted and checked deliveries against packing lists"
check.why: It uses an action word and a real task, and claims nothing you do not have.
